agentCan: Implement the authorization-code + PKCE flow and Management API calls
Design the scope set up front (the expensive decision) and the re-authorization communications
Handle revocation (refresh failures, 401s) and per-app rate-limit backoff

approval.trigger: None described: the integration guide and Management API reference describe no review, approval, listing, marketplace, user cap, or fee for OAuth Apps. You create the app in your organization settings and users can authorize it; the guide's phrase 'once you've published your OAuth App' refers to having created it, not to an approval gate.

blockers.detail: Scopes are configured when you CREATE the OAuth app; the authorize URL's scope parameter is explicitly deprecated. 'You can update scopes of your OAuth app at any time, but existing OAuth app users will need to re-authorize your app via the OAuth flow to apply the new scopes.' Every scope change is a re-consent campaign across your installed base.
blockers.howToClear: Choose the complete scope set carefully at creation; batch any changes and communicate them as an upgrade.
blockers.title: Scopes are fixed at creation; changes force re-authorization

blockers.detail: The Management API's standard limit (120 requests per minute, per user, per project or organization, per endpoint) changes shape for OAuth apps: 'the limit applies to the app, shared by everyone calling through it', tracked by OAuth App ID. Heavy multi-user traffic through one app shares one ceiling.
blockers.howToClear: Cache aggressively, batch calls, and back off per app, not per user.
blockers.title: Rate limits attach to your app, shared by all users

blockers.detail: 'You cannot retrieve the database password via the management API.' For a user's existing projects, direct database access means collecting their DB password in your own UI; for projects you create via the API, you must supply or generate the password and store it securely yourself.
blockers.howToClear: Decide whether you truly need direct DB access; if you do, budget the credential-collection UX and its security review.
blockers.title: The database password is unreachable

alternatives: OAuth 2.1 Server in Supabase Auth: makes YOUR Supabase-built project an identity provider (third parties 'sign in with' your app). The reverse direction; also notable because you must build the consent UI yourself and its scopes do not limit data access. Not the flavor for connecting users' Supabase projects
flavor.recommended: A Management API OAuth App, registered in your own Supabase organization's settings (OAuth Apps tab)
flavor.why: The Management API reference frames it directly: 'Use this if you're building a third-party app that needs to create or manage Supabase projects on behalf of your users.' Users authorize the app and it receives access and refresh tokens for the Management API on their behalf. Do not confuse this with Supabase Auth's OAuth 2.1 Server, which points the other way (see alternatives).

humanMust: Create the OAuth App in your organization's settings and set its scopes at creation
Custody the client ID and secret
Supply/store database passwords for any projects your app creates via the API
name: Supabase
nuances: Scope categories are powerful and coarse: Secrets: Read includes retrieving a project's API keys and secrets; Database: Write includes running SQL queries and disabling read-only mode for 15 minutes.

Fine-grained access control is not fully rolled out: the guide warns 'only some features are available until we roll out fine-grained access control', and tokens effectively grant broad Management API access within the chosen scopes.
redirect_uri and state together cannot exceed 4kB; an optional organization_slug parameter pre-selects the user's organization at authorize time.
If a user revokes access, refresh fails and access tokens stop working; the docs instruct handling HTTP Unauthorized errors on any Supabase API call.
PKCE (S256) is 'strongly recommended' and the client secret travels as a Basic auth header at the token endpoint.
prerequisites: The full scope set, decided up front (changes force re-authorization)

steps.detail: In your organization's settings, OAuth Apps tab > Add application: fill in the required details and configure the app's scopes NOW (Auth, Database, Domains, Edge Functions, Environment, Organizations, Projects, Rest, Secrets, Storage; read/write each). Click Confirm; receive the client ID and client secret.
steps.title: Create the OAuth App (scopes set here, permanently)

steps.detail: Add a 'Connect Supabase' button in your UI (Supabase points integrators to its brand-asset guidelines) that starts the flow.
steps.title: Add the connect entry point

steps.detail: Redirect the user to api.supabase.com/v1/oauth/authorize with client_id, redirect_uri, response_type=code, state (redirect_uri + state together cannot exceed 4kB), optional organization_slug to pre-select their organization, and PKCE code_challenge (S256, strongly recommended).
steps.title: Redirect the user to authorize

steps.detail: POST to api.supabase.com/v1/oauth/token (form-encoded grant_type=authorization_code, code, identical redirect_uri, code_verifier if PKCE), with client ID and secret as a Basic auth header. Returns access and refresh tokens.
steps.title: Exchange the code

steps.detail: Call the Management API with Authorization: Bearer <access_token>; refresh via the same token endpoint. Note the rate limit applies to your app across all users, and handle revocation: a revoked user's refresh fails and their access tokens stop working.
steps.title: Call the Management API

tagline: Two OAuth programs pointing in opposite directions; the integration one (Management API OAuth Apps) has no review, but its scopes are set at app creation and any change forces every existing user to re-authorize.

time.active: ~10 min of dashboard setup + ~1-2 hrs of standard flow code
